clue.text: The birds that are likely to be plucked

definitions.meaning: small migratory songbirds of open country, with a white rump

definitions.text: that are likely to be plucked
definitions.meaning: heads of grain on cereal stalks, which are picked off by hand, as the disciples did on the Sabbath

explanation.surface: Some poor birds are destined to have their feathers pulled out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plucked' suggests feathers, which fits the birds, but the second sense is the grain heads of a cereal crop being picked.
explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: one sense names a songbird species, the other the grain heads of a cereal crop that get picked off the stalk.

clue.text: He hasn't much regard for his betters

definitions.text: He hasn't much regard for his betters

parts.words: He hasn't much regard for his betters
parts.note: betters suggests social superiors, but here it means people who place bets, whom a dishonest bookmaker fails to pay

explanation.walkthrough: 'Betters' looks like 'superiors', but it means punters: someone who reneges on paying out to people who bet with them.
explanation.definitionFit: A bookmaker or gambler who fails to pay debts on wagers shows scant respect for the punters who placed them.

clue.text: With this, art doesn't lack support

definitions.text: With this, art doesn't lack support

parts.words: With this, art doesn't lack support
parts.note: sounds like arts funding, but the support is physical: a stand holding a canvas

explanation.walkthrough: 'Support' suggests patronage or funding for the arts, but it is a painter's wooden stand holding the canvas upright.
explanation.definitionFit: A painter's frame stand holds the canvas while a picture is worked on, so the artwork is propped up.

clue.text: Big game is his speciality

parts.note: big game suggests hunting large animals, but here it is the most important kind of cricket match, an international between national teams

explanation.walkthrough: 'Big game' sounds like a lion hunt, but in cricket the biggest game is a Test match, a five-day international, and this sportsman is picked for those.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricketer chosen for international five-day matches specialises in the most important fixtures of the sport.

clue.text: The fellow who was usually on watch

definitions.text: The fellow who was usually on watch

parts.words: The fellow who was usually on watch
parts.note: on watch suggests a sentry, but here it means attached to a pocket watch: a watch chain

explanation.walkthrough: 'On watch' suggests a guard; it is a heavy watch chain worn across a waistcoat, named after Queen Victoria's consort, and 'fellow' plays on its being a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's first name doubles as the term for a waistcoat watch chain, popularised by Victoria's husband.

clue.text: One who might be described as painstaking

definitions.text: One who might be described as painstaking

parts.words: One who might be described as painstaking
parts.note: painstaking normally means meticulous, but split up it means taking pains, enduring hurt

explanation.walkthrough: 'Painstaking' means careful, but read as 'pains-taking' it describes someone enduring pain.
explanation.definitionFit: A person enduring illness or hardship is literally taking pains, which splits the adjective into its parts.

clue.text: Not so hot

parts.note: read as a temperature, something lukewarm; read colloquially, something unimpressive

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase works both ways: lukewarm water, and a lukewarm reception or a performance that is not up to much.
explanation.definitionFit: Lukewarm liquid is neither hot nor cold, and a half-hearted welcome is called lukewarm too.

clue.text: To be or not to be the bride of. Pyramus

definitions.text: To be or not to be the bride of. Pyramus

parts.words: To be or not to be the bride of. Pyramus
parts.note: Pyramus's beloved in Ovid is ...; with the two letters of the verb 'to be' added she is named, without them only a short pointing word is left

explanation.walkthrough: The Hamlet line misleads: in Ovid, Pyramus loves Thisbe. Add 'be' to the answer and she appears; not adding 'be' leaves this four-letter word.
explanation.definitionFit: The demonstrative word is the beloved's name with its final two letters removed, so it is her name when 'to be' is absent.

clue.text: By no means distinguished

parts.note: by no means suggests not at all, but here means is money: someone marked out by having none

explanation.walkthrough: 'By no means' looks like 'not at all', but 'means' is wealth, so this is a person distinguished by having no money.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with no money at all is set apart by lacking any funds.

clue.text: " He treasures up His bright —, And works His sovereign Will" (Cowper)

definitions.text: He treasures up His bright —, And works His sovereign Will" (Cowper)

parts.words: He treasures up His bright —, And works His sovereign Will" (Cowper)
parts.note: the missing word after bright in Cowper's hymn God Moves in a Mysterious Way, plans held in unfathomable mines

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank: William Cowper's hymn reads 'Deep in unfathomable mines / Of never failing skill / He treasures up His bright ___ / And works His sovereign will.'
explanation.definitionFit: In the hymn, God stores up radiant plans or purposes, the intentions he carries out.

clue.text: Goes on and on having a snob value

definitions.meaning: continues, endures for a long time
snob is an old word for a cobbler or shoemaker, and the foot-shaped wooden blocks he shapes shoes on are what he values

explanation.surface: Something keeps going and going because it carries social cachet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snob' in old usage, still met in crosswords, is a cobbler; the second definition means the shoemaker's foot-shaped blocks, things of value to him, not social cachet.
explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: the verb means endures, and the noun is the cobbler's wooden foot models.

clue.text: Superfluous advice, in a word, to Quakers

definitions.text: Superfluous advice, in a word, to Quakers

parts.words: Superfluous advice, in a word, to Quakers
parts.note: Quakers belong to the Religious Society of Friends, so telling them to be on friendly terms is pointless; split two words

explanation.surface: Someone offers pointless guidance, in one word, to members of the Society of Friends.
explanation.walkthrough: Quakers are formally the Society of Friends, so advising them to 'be Friends' is superfluous; 'in a word' says the two words run together into one verb meaning makes friends with.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means offers friendship to someone; read as two words it is advice to join the Friends, which Quakers already are.

clue.text: Drink served in the vestibule ?

parts.note: porter is a dark beer, and one served in the entrance hall would be a hall's porter; the real sense is the doorman of a hotel or college

explanation.surface: A pint of dark beer is handed out in the entrance lobby.
explanation.walkthrough: Porter is a dark stout-like beer, but here the porter is the attendant at the door of a hotel or college, who serves people in the entrance hall.
explanation.definitionFit: The attendant stationed at a building's entrance, carrying luggage and directing visitors, works in the entrance area the clue calls a vestibule.

clue.text: He gets a degree in baking

annotationWithheld.why: Held answer RING does not fit 'He gets a degree in baking': the wordplay reads KING (He) taking BA (a degree) to make BAKING, so the answer looks like KING with an unchecked first letter misread; no parse gives RING.
annotationWithheld.clue: He gets a degree in baking

clue.text: Where, no doubt, current affairs are discussed

definitions.text: Where, no doubt, current affairs are discussed

parts.words: Where, no doubt, current affairs are discussed
parts.note: current affairs suggests news, but here current is electricity, generated in a power station, punning on a debating House

explanation.walkthrough: 'Current affairs' sounds like news topics, but the current is electrical, and a 'house' is also a debating chamber.
explanation.definitionFit: A generating station produces electric current, and the term also means an energetic, forceful person.

clue.text: Allow Peter a second performance

indicators.note: to allow Peter is to give him free rein, so his letters together with the a are let loose to rearrange

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to let Peter take the stage a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Allow' reads as a request for permission, but it frees the letters of PETER and A to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing a show again is a rerun, an encore staging of the same piece.

clue.text: Loss that can be pried into

indicators.note: says the letters of pried into could become something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: A loss is something that can be prised open and investigated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That can be' rearranges PRIED INTO.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruin or damnation, utter loss of the soul, is the theological meaning.

clue.text: They're a shifty lot

parts.note: shifty suggests dishonest people, but here the people shift things: furniture carriers who move house contents

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shifty' looks like 'untrustworthy', but the lot in question shift furniture for a living.
explanation.definitionFit: Firms of furniture carriers shift household goods from one home to another, so they are literally shifting people.

clue.text: They never get drunk

parts.note: suggests teetotallers, but these are the dregs left in the bottom of a glass, which nobody drinks

explanation.walkthrough: 'Get drunk' suggests people staying sober; it is the dregs of liquor left at the bottom of a glass, which go undrunk.
explanation.definitionFit: The leftover dregs at the base of a glass are never swallowed.

clue.text: Is he continually on edge?

parts.note: on edge suggests a nervous person; read literally, it is someone living on a boundary or frontier

explanation.walkthrough: 'On edge' means anxious, but here it means living at the edge of a country, especially along the frontier between England and Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who lives near the frontier between two countries, such as the Anglo-Scottish border, lives at a country's edge.

clue.text: Iagoo was the great one

definitions.note: in Longfellow's Song of Hiawatha, Iagoo is the great teller of tall tales and braggart

explanation.walkthrough: Iagoo, not Shakespeare's Iago, is the character in Longfellow's Song of Hiawatha, famous for exaggerated stories about himself.
explanation.definitionFit: Iagoo is described in the poem as a great braggart who told tall tales of his own exploits.

clue.text: A steed treated with a comb ?

definitions.text: A steed treated with a comb ?

indicators.note: the letters of a steed are treated, that is processed or worked over, and come out in a new order

explanation.surface: A horse is groomed with a curry comb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Treated' rearranges A STEED. The whole clue is also the definition: hair or wool worked over with a comb, as a groomed horse's mane would be.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair or fibres combed up or backcombed into a fluffed mass are said to have been worked over this way.

clue.text: Runs away to waste, as it were

explanation.surface: Someone flees and lets things go to ruin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waste' is a noun: arid wastelands. 'As it were' flags that the second sense is a noun plural.
explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: a soldier absconding from service, and barren sandy regions such as the Sahara.

clue.text: Matthew Arnold called him the Philistine of Genius in Literature

definitions.text: Matthew Arnold called him the Philistine of Genius in Literature

parts.words: Matthew Arnold called him the Philistine of Genius in Literature
parts.note: the Victorian critic applied this phrase to the author of The Pilgrim's Progress

explanation.walkthrough: A general-knowledge clue: Arnold used the phrase of John Bunyan, the 17th-century Puritan who wrote The Pilgrim's Progress.
explanation.definitionFit: The Puritan writer of The Pilgrim's Progress is the person the Victorian critic so described.

clue.text: A way of mine

parts.note: sounds like someone describing their own habit, but it is a passage into a mine

explanation.walkthrough: 'Of mine' looks like 'belonging to me'; here it means a pit, and the way is a horizontal entrance tunnel into it.
explanation.definitionFit: A horizontal passage driven into a hillside gives access to a mine for workers and drainage.

clue.text: No doubt they can recount harrowing experiences

definitions.text: No doubt they can recount harrowing experiences

parts.words: No doubt they can recount harrowing experiences
parts.note: harrowing suggests distressing, but here it is farm work: breaking up ploughed soil with a harrow

explanation.walkthrough: 'Harrowing' means distressing, but a harrow is the farm implement drawn over ploughed land, so the young farm lads have done it.
explanation.definitionFit: Lads who worked the plough on farms would also drag the harrow over the furrows, so they could tell of such work.

clue.text: Form of chore for a painter

indicators.note: a form of a word is that word reshaped, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Painting is a form of chore for an artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Form of' rearranges CHORE.
explanation.definitionFit: This yellowish-brown earth pigment is something an artist uses.

clue.text: However well brought up, they can't help being beastly to one another

definitions.text: However well brought up, they can't help being beastly to one another

parts.words: However well brought up, they can't help being beastly to one another
parts.note: beastly suggests nasty, but here it means being young animals to each other

explanation.walkthrough: 'Beastly' suggests rudeness, but young bears or lions are beasts to one another; well-raised Scout juniors share the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Young bears, foxes or lions are animals, and junior Scouts are also called by this name.

clue.text: Subject to payment for supplying water

definitions.meaning: a state obliged to pay tribute to a stronger one
a stream feeding a larger river or lake

explanation.surface: A water supply comes with charges attached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subject' is an adjective here: a vassal state paying tribute to an overlord; 'for' links the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: one sense is a vassal owing tribute, the other a stream flowing into a larger river.

clue.text: Doorkeeper in a tumble-down house ?

definitions.meaning: an official who shows people in at a door, as in a court or church
Poe's tale The Fall of the House of ... ends with the family mansion collapsing

explanation.surface: A doorman works in a dilapidated building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tumble-down' means more than dilapidated: in Edgar Allan Poe's story the family house literally falls into the tarn.
explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: one who shows guests to their seats, and the family name in Poe's story of a house that collapses.

clue.text: They could be opening payments

definitions.meaning: tears or splits in cloth, which are openings
regular sums paid to a landlord

explanation.surface: Some charges might be the first instalments due.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening payments' reads as first instalments, but split after 'opening': tears in fabric, and sums paid to a landlord.
explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: tears in fabric are gaps, and the sums a tenant pays a landlord are regular charges.

clue.text: Out of touch ? Could be !

parts.note: out of touch suggests behind the times, but literally it means without the sense of touch, or of any of the five faculties

explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of touch' means unaware of current trends; the 'Could be!' points to a literal reading: deprived of touch and the other faculties, as when unconscious.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone knocked unconscious has lost all feeling and perception, and the word also means foolish or pointless.
